{"id": "ad416c71-978c-4acf-8fd7-29affb69c852", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What is the difference between an Application Load Balancer and a Network Load Balancer?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "cbcd760a-8fdf-4230-8570-1fd64aee1886", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "thinking", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "This is a general AWS conceptual question about ALB vs NLB, not specific to the DevOps Agent product, so I'm confident answering directly from general AWS knowledge without needing special verification.\n\n"}]}

{"id": "56db6474-a2e3-4f4a-bcd6-3b4a25cca0d4", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Both are Elastic Load Balancing types. They work at different layers of the network stack.

| | **Application Load Balancer (ALB)** | **Network Load Balancer (NLB)** |
|---|---|---|
| **OSI layer** | Layer 7 (application) | Layer 4 (transport) |
| **Protocols** | HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket | TCP, UDP, TLS, TCP_UDP |
| **Routing** | Content-aware: host, path, headers, query strings, HTTP methods, source IP | Based on IP protocol data (port and protocol). It doesn't inspect the payload. |
| **Performance** | Good for web traffic, with slightly higher latency | Very high throughput and ultra-low latency. It handles millions of requests per second and sudden traffic spikes. |
| **IP addressing** | DNS name only. IPs can change. | One static IP per AZ, and you can attach Elastic IPs. This works well for IP allow-listing. |
| **Targets** | Instances, IPs, Lambda functions | Instances, IPs, and ALBs (an NLB can front an ALB) |
| **TLS** | Terminates TLS, with SNI and multiple certificates | Can terminate or pass through TLS |
| **Client IP preservation** | Passed in the `X-Forwarded-For` header | Preserved at the network level by default for instance targets |
| **Security groups** | Supported | Supported. You choose this when you create the NLB, and older NLBs created without it can't always add it later. |
| **Extra features** | Authentication (Cognito/OIDC), WAF integration, redirects, fixed responses, weighted target groups | PrivateLink (as the endpoint service front end), static IPs |

**Choose an ALB when:**
- You're serving HTTP/HTTPS or gRPC, such as web apps, microservices, or container-based APIs.
- You need path- or host-based routing, for example `/api` to one service and `/web` to another.
- You want WAF, built-in authentication, or Lambda targets.

**Choose an NLB when:**
- You need extreme performance or low latency, or have bursty, high-volume traffic.
- You're handling non-HTTP protocols such as raw TCP or UDP (gaming, IoT, DNS, custom protocols).
- You need static or Elastic IPs, or you're exposing a service through AWS PrivateLink.

You can also combine them. Putting an NLB in front of an ALB gives you static IPs and PrivateLink support while keeping Layer 7 routing.

If you want, I can look at the load balancers in your account and check which type fits each workload.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
